title: LLM Lab: choosing AI models on our own terms

beats.title: Every week, a new #1
beats.notes: Every week a new AI model claims to be the best.

beats.title: Best on what?
beats.notes: But best on whose data? Best for which job? And best at what price?

beats.title: LLM Lab
beats.notes: We built LLM Lab so we can answer those questions ourselves, with our own data and by our own rules.

beats.title: Leaderboard
beats.notes: Most companies choose models in one of three ways: a public leaderboard,

beats.title: Sales deck, first team
beats.notes: a vendor's sales deck, or whatever the first team happened to use.

beats.title: Into production
beats.notes: Whichever way, a model ends up in production.

beats.title: One weakness
beats.notes: All three share one weakness: the test wasn't ours.

beats.title: Someone else's test
beats.notes: A public benchmark measures someone else's documents, someone else's languages and someone else's idea of good.

beats.title: Our language
beats.notes: A model that tops the charts in English may struggle with Polish support tickets.

beats.title: Two points, thirty times
beats.notes: A model that's two points better might cost thirty times more.

beats.title: Nobody checks
beats.notes: And once a model is in production, nobody checks whether it's still the right choice.

beats.title: Our data
beats.notes: Our data. The test cases come from our own work: real support questions, real contracts, real tickets.

beats.title: In our repository
beats.notes: They live in our own repository and get reviewed like code.

beats.title: Our criteria
beats.notes: Our criteria. We decide what good enough means.

beats.title: High bar for personal data
beats.notes: For detecting personal data the bar is high, because a miss is a compliance incident. For product search it can be lower.

beats.title: Our decision
beats.notes: Our decision. A model we call through an API and a model we host ourselves face exactly the same tests.

beats.title: Plan B
beats.notes: If a provider raises prices or changes its terms, we already know our next-best option and what it costs.

elements.text: RAG: ANSWERS FROM OUR OWN DOCUMENTS
wrong chunks in = a confident wrong answer out

beats.title: What RAG is
beats.notes: Most of what we build answers from our own documents. It's called RAG: retrieval-augmented generation. The language model doesn't know our contracts; we find the right pages and hand them over.

beats.title: Preparing documents
beats.notes: First we prepare the documents: chunking cuts them into pieces that make sense on their own, and an embedding model turns every piece into numbers, so similar meanings end up close together.

beats.title: A question comes in
beats.notes: When a question comes in, we turn it into numbers the same way and look for the closest chunks.

beats.title: Rerank, then answer
beats.notes: Search is fast but rough, so a reranker reads the top fifty and puts the best ones first. Only the top five reach the language model that writes the answer.

beats.title: Classification at the front door
beats.notes: And before any of that, a classifier decides what the message is about, how urgent it is, and whether it contains personal data.

beats.title: The quality is decided here
beats.notes: If the chunks are bad or the search misses, the best language model in the world answers from the wrong page. These four small steps decide the quality, and they run on every document and every question.

beats.title: Why these four?
beats.notes: Why these four? Because we only test models where our own data can change the answer: models that are worth fine-tuning.

beats.title: Big models: prompt, don't tune
beats.notes: A frontier language model is huge, general, and replaced every few months. We use it through prompts and RAG; fine-tuning it ourselves rarely pays off.

beats.title: Building blocks: tune them
beats.notes: The building blocks are different. They do one narrow job, millions of times. A small open model trained on a few thousand of our own examples can match a big one at a fraction of the cost.

beats.title: The numbers
beats.notes: On our support intents, a fine-tuned ModernBERT matches Claude Sonnet within the noise, at less than half a cent per thousand tickets instead of a dollar.

beats.title: The rule
beats.notes: So the rule is simple: if a model is worth fine-tuning, it's worth testing here, against the API models, on exactly the same cases.

beats.title: The lab
beats.notes: We're starting with four types of models, the building blocks behind search, assistants and automation.

beats.title: Embedding
beats.notes: Embedding models turn text into numbers, so we can find the documents that match a question.

beats.title: Chunking
beats.notes: Chunking splits long documents into pieces that make sense on their own.

beats.title: Reranking
beats.notes: Reranking takes the top search results and puts the best answer first.

beats.title: Classification
beats.notes: Classification sorts incoming items: what the customer wants, how urgent it is, whether the message contains personal data.

beats.title: Built to grow
beats.notes: More categories will follow. The lab is built to grow.

beats.title: Why this model?
beats.notes: This gives us decisions we can explain. When someone asks why this model,

beats.title: Not a leaderboard
beats.notes: the answer isn't: it was top of a leaderboard.

beats.title: Evidence
beats.notes: It's: it passed our tests, on our data, at this price, and here's the evidence.

beats.title: A new model comes out
beats.notes: And when a new model comes out, we add it, run it, and the lab shows us whether it's worth switching.
